posts.title: Understanding BGP Security: From Academic Research to Real-World Implications
posts.excerpt: Insights from researching BGP routing vulnerabilities and prefix hijacking attacks in Autonomous Systems.
posts.content:
During my research fellowship at FURG, I investigated one of the internet's most critical yet invisible security challenges: BGP routing vulnerabilities. This research resulted in two published papers and an award for academic excellence.

## What is BGP and Why Should Developers Care?

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol that makes the internet work. It's how Autonomous Systems exchange routing information to direct traffic across the global network. But here's the problem: BGP was designed in a time when trust was assumed, not verified.

## The Security Challenge

Prefix hijacking occurs when a malicious actor announces BGP routes they don't own, effectively redirecting internet traffic. This isn't theoretical—it happens regularly and can affect entire regions.

My research focused on analyzing these vulnerabilities, studying traffic engineering patterns, and understanding how attacks propagate through Autonomous Systems.

## What I Learned

### 1. Infrastructure Matters More Than You Think

As application developers, we often take network infrastructure for granted. But understanding how routing actually works changes how you think about system design, latency, and failure modes.

### 2. Security is About the Whole Stack

You can build the most secure application in the world, but if the underlying network infrastructure is vulnerable, your users are at risk.

### 3. Research Methodology is Valuable for Engineers

The systematic thinking required for academic research—forming hypotheses, gathering data, analyzing results—directly applies to debugging production systems and architectural decision-making.

## Bridging Theory and Practice

This research wasn't just academic. Understanding network-layer vulnerabilities informs how I think about:
- Designing distributed systems
- Analyzing latency and performance issues
- Making security-conscious architectural decisions
- Debugging issues that span application and infrastructure layers

## Key Takeaways for Developers

- Learn beyond your primary domain—understanding infrastructure makes you a better application developer
- Security thinking should span all layers of the stack
- Academic research skills (analysis, documentation, methodology) are valuable in professional development
- The internet's fundamental protocols have real security implications for our applications

Publishing research and working on production systems has taught me that the best engineers understand both theory and practice.

posts.title: Lessons from Working on Production ERP Systems
posts.excerpt: What I've learned developing real business software that companies depend on daily.
posts.content:
Working at OneWeb Soluções Inteligentes has taught me something crucial: production software is different from personal projects. When real businesses depend on your code for daily operations, the stakes change completely.

## The Reality of Enterprise Software

ERP systems aren't glamorous. They're complex, business-critical applications handling inventory, sales, financial operations—the core of how companies function. When something breaks, it's not just a bug; it's blocking actual business operations.

## What Production Work Teaches You

### 1. Legacy Code is Real

Most codebases aren't greenfield projects with the latest tech stack. I work with CakePHP—both maintaining legacy code and implementing new features. This teaches you to work with what exists, not just what's ideal.

### 2. Data Integrity is Everything

In ERP systems, data integrity isn't optional. A mistake in inventory counts or financial calculations has real-world consequences. This forces careful thinking about transactions, validation, and edge cases.

### 3. Business Logic is Complex

Real-world business processes are messy. They have exceptions, special cases, and requirements that don't fit clean architectural patterns. Learning to balance code quality with business needs is crucial.

### 4. Users Don't Care About Your Tech Stack

Clients care about features working reliably, not whether you used the newest framework. This recalibrates your priorities—deliver value, not just technically elegant solutions.

## MySQL/MariaDB in Production

Working with production databases teaches you:
- Query optimization matters at scale
- Indexing strategies affect real performance
- Backups aren't theoretical—they're essential
- Understanding ACID properties isn't academic

## Bridging Modern and Legacy

One valuable skill is working with both legacy systems and modern practices. You learn to:
- Refactor carefully without breaking existing functionality
- Add tests to code that didn't have them
- Improve systems incrementally, not just rebuild from scratch
- Balance technical debt against feature delivery

## What This Means for Career Growth

Production experience is different from side projects:
- You learn to work within constraints
- You understand the full lifecycle of features
- You gain empathy for maintainability
- You see the consequences of technical decisions

Working on real systems serving real users is the fastest way to grow as a developer.

posts.title: Building in Public: The Architecture Behind This Portfolio
posts.excerpt: How I applied Clean Architecture principles to build this portfolio site with Next.js and TypeScript.
posts.content:
This portfolio isn't just a showcase—it's a demonstration of architectural thinking. I built it using Clean Architecture, comprehensive testing, and modern web technologies.

## Why Architecture Matters for a Portfolio

Most portfolio sites are simple static pages. But I wanted to demonstrate that I think about systems architecture, not just individual features. This site is intentionally over-engineered to showcase skills.

## Clean Architecture Implementation

### Core Layer: Entities and Value Objects
Business logic lives in pure TypeScript classes: `Project`, `WorkExperience`, `Skill`, `BlogPost`. These have no framework dependencies.

### Use Cases Layer
Applications services like `GetAllProjects`, `GetProfile`, `CheckColorContrast` contain business rules. They're framework-agnostic and testable.

### Adapters Layer
Repositories, theme management, i18n—these connect core business logic to external systems. They implement ports defined by the core.

### Presentation Layer
Next.js 14 with App Router, React Server Components, TypeScript. The UI layer depends on use cases, not the other way around.

## Technical Decisions

### Why Next.js 14?
- Modern React patterns (Server Components)
- Built-in internationalization support
- Excellent TypeScript support
- Static generation for GitHub Pages

### Why Clean Architecture?
- Demonstrates architectural thinking
- Makes testing easier (pure functions)
- Shows understanding beyond frameworks
- Prepares for scaling complexity

### Testing Strategy
- **Vitest** for unit tests (entities, use cases, value objects)
- **React Testing Library** for component integration tests
- **Playwright** for e2e flows
- **Cypress** for specialized testing (WCAG contrast)

## Accessibility & Internationalization

### WCAG AAA Compliance
Implemented comprehensive color contrast checking to meet AAA standards. This isn't just about compliance—it's about inclusive design.

### i18n Support
Full Portuguese and English support using next-intl. Content is completely separate from presentation logic.

## What I Learned

### 1. Over-Engineering Can Be Educational
Yes, this is over-engineered for a portfolio. But that's the point—it's a learning exercise and a demonstration.

### 2. Architecture Scales Down
Clean Architecture principles work even for small projects. The separation of concerns makes everything more testable.

### 3. Testing Gives Confidence
Comprehensive tests let me refactor fearlessly. I've restructured components multiple times without breaking functionality.

### 4. Documentation is Part of the Code
Extensive documentation (COMPONENT_ARCHITECTURE.md, QUICK_REFERENCE.md, etc.) makes the project maintainable.

## The Meta Lesson

Building this portfolio taught me that how you build something is often as important as what you build. The architecture, testing strategy, and documentation demonstrate professional software engineering practices.

Check out the code on GitHub to see the full implementation!
